interviewQuestions.question: What's the basic difference between a CPU, a GPU, and an ASIC like a TPU — why does specialization keep going further?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as a spectrum of trading generality for efficiency. A CPU is fully general: it can run any program, including ones nobody anticipated when the chip was designed, at the cost of spending a lot of its silicon on things that make arbitrary code fast (branch prediction, out-of-order execution, deep caches) rather than on raw compute throughput. A GPU narrows that generality to "lots of independent, uniform work" — it's still programmable (you write real kernels in CUDA or similar), but it commits its silicon to thousands of simple cores instead of a few complex ones, betting the workload has enough parallelism to keep them all busy.

An ASIC like a TPU narrows further still: instead of being programmable for a broad class of parallel problems, it's built for one specific computational pattern — for a TPU, large matrix multiplication — and wires that pattern directly into the hardware's dataflow rather than executing generic instructions at all. Each step down this spectrum (CPU to GPU to ASIC) trades away flexibility for efficiency on the narrower thing it's built for, and the efficiency gain compounds because the chip stops spending area and power on generality it doesn't need for that specific job.

The reason specialization keeps going further, historically: as a workload (like deep learning) matures from research curiosity to massive, stable, repeated production usage, the economic case for building hardware around its exact shape gets stronger — you're no longer guessing what future workloads might need, you're optimizing for a workload you already know precisely.

**Testing:** whether you understand the CPU-GPU-ASIC progression as one continuous flexibility-for-efficiency trade-off, not three unrelated categories of chip.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: The specialization spectrum

interviewQuestions.question: When would you choose a TPU or custom ASIC over a GPU for a machine learning workload?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame the decision around how stable and narrow the workload actually is. If a team is actively researching new model architectures — trying novel layer types, custom ops, unconventional attention mechanisms — a GPU's general programmability matters more than raw efficiency, because an ASIC's narrow, fixed operation set might not even be able to express what they're trying to build; iterating on a TPU-only architecture that doesn't support your new op means you're blocked on hardware, not just slower.

Once a model architecture is stable and running at massive scale — serving a well-established model billions of times a day, or repeatedly training the same architecture on new data — the workload becomes dominated by a fixed, well-understood computational pattern, usually large matrix multiplies at the core of transformer or CNN layers. That's exactly the profile a systolic-array-based TPU is built for, and the efficiency gain (often a substantial jump in performance-per-watt and per-dollar at scale) starts to outweigh the lost flexibility, especially once the cost of running that fixed workload at scale on general-purpose GPUs becomes the dominant line item in an infrastructure budget.

So my rule of thumb: research and iteration favor GPUs; stable, high-volume production inference or training of a fixed, well-characterized architecture favors TPUs/ASICs — and real organizations often run both, using GPUs for R&D and migrating the winning architecture to custom accelerators once it's proven and running at scale.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about the flexibility-vs-efficiency trade-off in a concrete business and workload-lifecycle context, not just recite that "TPUs are faster."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: GPU vs TPU decision

interviewQuestions.question: What is a systolic array and why is it used in accelerators like TPUs?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A systolic array is a grid of simple multiply-accumulate units arranged so that data flows through the grid in a fixed rhythm — each cell passes its partial result to a neighboring cell every cycle, like a heartbeat pumping blood through a network of vessels, which is where the name comes from. Critically, there's no instruction fetch or decode happening per step inside the array — the computation pattern itself is wired directly into the hardware's physical dataflow, not executed as a sequence of generic instructions the way a CPU or even a GPU core would.

This works exceptionally well specifically for matrix multiplication because that operation has an extremely regular, predictable data-access and computation pattern: every output element is a sum of products following the same fixed structure, and a systolic array's grid can be laid out so that each input value streams through the array exactly once, getting reused by multiple multiply-accumulate operations as it passes by, without ever needing to be re-fetched from memory. A GPU, by contrast, is also massively parallel but still issues instructions generically to each core even for this same regular pattern — a systolic array eliminates almost all of that control overhead by hardwiring the exact dataflow matrix multiply needs.

The trade-off, worth naming explicitly for a complete answer: this efficiency is tied entirely to that one dataflow pattern — a systolic array isn't a general parallel computer that happens to be fast at matrix multiply, it's a physical embodiment of one specific algorithm's structure, which is exactly why it can't flexibly run the wide variety of operations a GPU kernel can.

**Testing:** whether you understand the actual mechanism behind the efficiency claim (fixed dataflow eliminating control overhead), not just that "TPUs are good at matrix multiply."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: How systolic arrays achieve efficiency
